Review 1: Flags this as the “most obvious confound”: the extra money itself could improve happiness, particularly for lower-income participants. Suggests equal payments or checking heterogeneity by income. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Flags essentially the same issue as an IV exclusion-restriction problem: assignment changes both deactivation and expected compensation, so assignment could affect emotional state through money rather than deactivation.
Comparison: Strong agreement. Review 1 explains the intuitive confound; Review 2 gives the econometric version. This concern is directly grounded in the design: the paper acknowledges that treatment and control differed in both deactivation length and total payment.

Review 1: Strong critique. Notes that outcomes are subjective, participants know their assignment, and enthusiasm about deactivation could influence reporting. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Does not make this a major criticism. Its concerns about the outcome focus more on standardization and timing.
Comparison: Review 1 caught something Review 2 largely missed. The paper itself acknowledges that knowledge of participation could influence survey answers and that it relies on three self-reported questions.

Issue: Deviation from the original European Social Survey items
Review 1: Detailed criticism: the paper changes the recall window from one week to four weeks and changes the response scale/labels. Review 1 argues that “often/sometimes/rarely” may measure frequency of episodes differently from duration over time. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Does not identify this construct-validity issue.
Comparison: Review 1 only. This is one of Review 1’s most distinctive substantive points. The paper says its questions were “drawn from” and “similar to” the ESS measure, not identical.

Review 1: Treats it as an important red flag, especially because emotional state was later spun into a separate paper. Raises regression-to-the-mean and residual confounding concerns. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Notices the same imbalance, but asks a narrower technical question: was baseline emotional state guaranteed to enter the LASSO-adjusted regression rather than potentially being penalized out?
Comparison: Agreement on the factual issue, different diagnosis. Review 1 questions inference/selection; Review 2 questions reproducibility of the adjustment. The paper confirms a chance baseline imbalance in Facebook and says baseline emotional state was controlled for.

Issue: Splitting the preregistered project into two papers
Review 1: Raises this as a possible researcher-degrees-of-freedom / selective-emphasis issue because emotional state was originally a secondary outcome and happened to show an interesting result. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Records the preregistration architecture and scrutinizes multiple testing but does not push the selective-publication interpretation nearly as far.
Comparison: Mostly Review 1. The paper explicitly says the PAP originally implied one paper, that the results were subsequently split, and that emotional state was a secondary outcome.

Review 1: Raises the broad concern: asks whether the authors adhered to their promised 0.05 threshold and whether post-preregistration changes weaken the evidential claim. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Much more precise. Identifies that the paper calls the adjusted Instagram result a “p = 0.14” when the procedure actually produces an FDR-adjusted q-value, and separately notes that exploratory subgroup tests use unadjusted p-values across many moderators.
Comparison: Substantial agreement, but Review 2 catches the technical reporting error Review 1 misses. The paper says its PAP called for sharpened FDR q-values across 61 outcomes and unadjusted subgroup p-values.

Review 1: Major theme. Emphasizes that 0.041–0.060 SD is small and translates the original-scale effects to roughly 3.8% of respondents shifting one response category. Warns against equating statistical significance with practical importance. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Generally accepts the paper’s effect-size benchmarking and instead audits whether the calculations are correct.
Comparison: Review 1 provides the stronger interpretive critique. Review 2 is more of a numerical auditor here.

Review 1: Does not catch the arithmetic error.
Review 2: Catches a concrete mistake: Facebook = 0.060/0.27 ≈ 22%, Instagram = 0.041/0.27 ≈ 15%, whereas the manuscript says “15 and 22 percent,” reversing them.
Comparison: Review 2 only—and this looks like a genuine manuscript error. The underlying paper text indeed gives the reversed 15/22 ordering.

Issue: Timing of outcome measurement after accounts were reactivated
Review 1: Does not notice it.
Review 2: Flags that treatment accounts were reactivated Nov. 4, while endline ran Nov. 4–18 and asked about the past four weeks. Late respondents therefore reported on as much as two weeks after reactivation, diluting the treatment contrast. It also connects this to differential survey timing around the Nov. 7 election call.
Comparison: Review 2 only. This is a substantive design issue, not merely a typo. The paper confirms Nov. 4–18 endline fielding, Nov. 4 reactivation, and the four-week recall measure.

Issue: IV compliance measure captures login days, not usage intensity
Review 1: Missed.
Review 2: Notes that the instrumented deactivation variable uses whether someone viewed ≥5 pieces of content on a day. Assignment could also reduce minutes used on “active” days, creating a treatment channel not represented in the compliance measure.
Comparison: Review 2 only. The paper defines compliance from the share of days crossing that content threshold, not minutes of use.

Issue: One-week control deactivation may change later control behavior
Review 1: Missed.
Review 2: Raises possible rebound/re-entry effects after controls reactivate on Sept. 30. If the control arm is behaviorally altered by its week of abstention, it may not represent ordinary Facebook/Instagram use.
Comparison: Review 2 only. This is a thoughtful identification issue rather than a demonstrated bias.

Issue: Different age cutoffs for Facebook and Instagram subgroups
Review 1: Mentions subgroup effects but does not notice the comparability problem.
Review 2: Points out that “young” means 18–34 for Facebook but 18–24 for Instagram, making cross-platform statements about age heterogeneity potentially misleading. Suggests harmonized bins.
Comparison: Review 2 only. Particularly important because the abstract juxtaposes “over 35” Facebook effects with “women under 25” Instagram effects.

Issue: Exploratory subgroup claims are weakly supported statistically
Review 1: Broadly warns about searching among subgroups and statistical flexibility. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Quantifies the issue: some highlighted heterogeneity tests are around p=.046, .053, .058, and the Instagram omnibus gender×age test is p=.062, all without multiplicity correction.
Comparison: Agreement, with Review 2 substantially more precise. The paper openly labels these analyses non-preregistered and uses unadjusted p-values.

Review 1: Missed.
Review 2: Flags that eligibility requires ≥85% nonmissing tracking during a post-randomization period, and asks whether weighting was re-estimated for this selected 25–29% subsample.
Comparison: Review 2 only. The paper confirms that the tracking sample uses post-intervention completeness criteria.

Review 1: Missed.
Review 2: Asks exactly what “sample-weighted combined Control groups” means: pooled platforms? which wave? same reference distribution across waves?
Comparison: Review 2 only. More of a reproducibility/documentation issue than a clear threat to the estimate.

Review 1: Missed.
Review 2: Asks whether baseline outcomes were forced into the model, how λ was chosen, whether weights entered selection, and why ordinary outcome-selection rather than a double-selection procedure was used.
Comparison: Review 2 only. A technical econometric point.

Review 1: Missed.
Review 2: Notes that the paper claims the 18–24 Instagram effect is 17% of the historical Kessler-6 trend without giving the pooled 18–24 estimate needed to reproduce that number.
Comparison: Review 2 only. A transparency/reproducibility catch.

Review 1: Missed.
Review 2: Notes ambiguity over whether “bounds exclude zero” refers to bound point estimates or confidence intervals around the bounds.
Comparison: Review 2 only. Technically important for how strong the robustness claim is.

Review 1: Largely not the purpose of Review 1.
Review 2: Finds many: ≥15 vs >15 minutes, misplaced parenthesis, “respectively,.”, equation notation, wrong comparison group (“non-college”), publication years in Figure 3, subject–verb agreement, bibliography issues, etc.
Comparison: Review 2 overwhelmingly stronger. These are mostly editorial rather than threats to the paper’s central result.

Review 1: Central concern. Review 1 repeatedly asks whether the combination of secondary outcomes, baseline imbalance, subgroup searches, and paper-splitting could reflect pressure to produce a positive story. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Does not infer author motivation and stays much closer to identifiable statistical or reporting issues.
Comparison: Review 1 only. This is also the most interpretive/speculative portion of Review 1, so it deserves more caution than its concrete measurement and payment critiques.

Review 1: Raises this as a take-home/bonus issue, referring to undisclosed connections discussed elsewhere. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Mentions related Meta work/literature but does not make institutional conflict a major critique.
Comparison: Mostly Review 1. The paper itself discloses the Meta collaboration and says independent academics retained final authority over analysis and manuscript text.
